title: Graphic Communication
summary: Freehand sketching, types of lines, oblique and isometric drawings, first-angle orthographic projection, scale and dimensioning.

notes.text: **Graphic communication** is the use of drawings to share design ideas. Drawings can show the shape, size and details of a product much more clearly than words.

rows: Guidelines for drawing; erased or left faint
Edges that cannot be seen from that view
Thin, long dash and short dash
Centre of circles and symmetrical shapes
Thin with arrowheads at both ends

notes.title: Choosing the right line
notes.problem: Which type of line do you use for (a) the visible edge of a box, (b) an edge hidden behind it, (c) the centre of a hole, (d) your first light guide lines?
steps: (a) Visible edges are thick, continuous outlines.
(d) Construction lines are thin and faint.
notes.answer: Outline, hidden detail, centre line and construction line.

rows: The front view is drawn flat, true shape and size. Depth lines are drawn at **45°** to the horizontal, often at half their real length (cabinet oblique).
The object is turned so that an edge faces you. Vertical edges stay **vertical**; horizontal edges are drawn at **30°** to the horizontal. All measurements along the three axes are true length.
Lines meet at one or two vanishing points, making the object look realistic (used by artists and architects).

notes.text: **Orthographic projection** shows an object as several flat (2D) views, each seen straight on. In **first-angle orthographic projection** (used in South Africa):

items: The **top view** (plan) is drawn **below** the front view.
The **left view** is drawn on the **right** of the front view (the view from the left is placed on the right).

notes.label: Exam tip
notes.text: Views in orthographic projection must line up: the top view is directly below the front view, and the side view is level with the front view. Use faint projection lines to transfer sizes.

items: **1 : 1** (full size): the drawing is the same size as the object.
**1 : 2** (reduction): the drawing is half the real size. Used for large objects.
**2 : 1** (enlargement): the drawing is twice the real size. Used for small objects.
Dimensions are written in **millimetres (mm)**, without writing the unit, above the dimension line so they can be read from the bottom or the right of the page.

notes.title: Using scale
notes.problem: A table top is 1 200 mm long. How long is it on a drawing at a scale of 1 : 10?
